---

The crocodile, with cunning grin, reclined in the dentist's chair,
And declared, "Throughout my gleaming jaws, my teeth need urgent care."
The dentist's face grew ashen pale; he trembled, quaked, and shook.
He murmured faintly, "I suppose I'd better take a look."

"I wish," the Crocodile proclaimed, "you'd tend the back ones first—
Those distant molars, at the rear, are easily the worst."
He spread his massive jaws apart—a sight to fill with dread—
At least three hundred gleaming fangs, all pointed, sharp, and spread.

The dentist kept a wary distance, standing well away,
And chose his longest probe to seek the decay where it lay.
"I told you—see the back ones first!" the Crocodile complained.
"You're standing far too distant, sir, to see what must be gained.

To properly inspect the back, you must incline your head
Deep down within my cavernous mouth," the grinning reptile said.
The dentist wrung his trembling hands and, weeping in despair,
Cried out, "No, no! I see them clearly—perfectly—from here!"

Just then a lady burst inside, a golden chain in hand,
Exclaiming, "Oh, you mischievous Croc! Must you again pretend?"
"Watch out!" the dentist shrieked aloud, and scrambled up the wall.
"He means to eat us both alive! He's coming for us all!"

"Don't be absurd," the lady laughed, with a radiant, easy smile.
"He's perfectly harmless—merely my beloved crocodile."

**The Crocodile's Dental Visit**

With a sly grin spreading across his face, the crocodile settled into the dentist's chair. "Every single tooth in my mouth needs fixing," he announced, "from front to back, no exceptions."

The dentist's complexion drained to a ghostly pale. His whole body trembled with fright. "Well then," he stammered, "I suppose I have no choice but to examine them."

"Start with the ones in back," the crocodile insisted. "Those rear molars are by far the most troublesome." With that, he stretched his enormous jaws open, revealing a terrifying sight—hundreds upon hundreds of gleaming, razor-sharp teeth, easily three hundred or more.

Keeping a safe distance of several feet, the dentist refused to move closer. Instead, he grabbed his most extended dental probe, hoping to spot the cavities from afar.

"I told you to check the back teeth!" the crocodile protested loudly. "You can't possibly examine them properly from way over there, good sir. To do this right, you'll need to lean your entire head into my mouth," he explained, his grin widening mischievously.

Overcome with distress, the dentist twisted his hands together and began to sob. "Absolutely not! I can see perfectly fine from this position, thank you very much!"

At that moment, a woman burst through the door, clutching a golden leash. "Croc, you rascal!" she exclaimed. "Are you up to your pranks again?"

The dentist let out a terrified scream and scrambled up the wall in panic. "Run! He's coming for me—he'll get you too! We're all going to be eaten!"

The woman simply laughed and offered a warm smile. "Don't be silly," she said. "He wouldn't hurt a fly. This is just my darling pet crocodile."

# The Crocodile's Dental Visit

The bell above the door jingled cheerfully, utterly failing to prepare Dr. Whitmore for what shuffled into his dental clinic that Tuesday afternoon. A crocodile—a genuine, scaly, six-foot crocodile—waddled in on its stubby legs and hoisted itself into the waiting room chair with surprising delicacy.

"I need an emergency appointment," the crocodile announced, his voice a gravelly rumble. "My back molars are killing me. Absolute agony."

Dr. Whitmore, who had spent fifteen years treating everything from toddlers to the occasional nervous grandmother, found himself frozen behind his reception desk, pen suspended mid-air.

"Right this way," he managed to squeak, gesturing toward the examination room with considerably less enthusiasm than usual.

Once the crocodile had settled into the reclined chair—which groaned ominously under his weight—Dr. Whitmore approached with the longest probe he owned, holding it at arm's length like a fencer wary of an unpredictable opponent.

"Just open wide," he said, positioning himself a full three feet from those glistening rows of teeth, "and I'll take a look from here."

The crocodile obliged, jaws creaking open to reveal an intimidating cavern of ivory daggers. Dr. Whitmore leaned forward exactly two inches, squinted, and prodded uselessly at the air near the crocodile's front teeth.

"I can't see anything from way back here," the crocodile complained, his voice muffled but still perfectly clear. "You'll need to put your head right inside. All the way to the back. That's where it really hurts."

Dr. Whitmore's hand trembled. "Surely I could use a mirror, or perhaps an X-ray machine, or—"

"The *back* teeth," the crocodile insisted, jaws widening further, an unmistakable glint flickering in his reptilian eye. "You simply must get your whole head in there to see properly."

Sweat beaded on the dentist's forehead as he realized, with dawning horror, that this was no ordinary patient consultation. This was an invitation to become lunch.

Just as Dr. Whitmore began backing toward the door, the front bell jingled again, and a stern-looking woman burst into the room, brandishing a golden chain and wagging a finger with the authority of someone who had done this many times before.

"Oh no you don't!" she scolded, marching straight up to the crocodile. "Not this trick again! You promised me you'd behave yourself at the doctor's office!"

Dr. Whitmore, already halfway to the door, felt his panic spike to new heights. A crocodile was terrifying enough—but a crocodile with an *owner* who spoke to him like a misbehaving schoolboy? This was clearly some elaborate scheme, and he wanted no part of it.

"Please," he stammered, pressing himself against the wall, "I don't want any trouble, just take him and—"

"Oh, don't worry yourself, Doctor," the woman interrupted, clipping the golden chain gently onto a collar around the crocodile's thick neck. She smiled apologetically. "He's completely harmless, truly. This old rascal is my pet—he's just terribly fond of his little jokes. Aren't you, Snappy?"

The crocodile, looking rather sheepish for a creature of his size, let out what might have been a chuckle. "Worth a try," he muttered.

Dr. Whitmore exhaled a breath he hadn't realized he'd been holding, his heart rate slowly returning to something resembling normal. He looked between the woman's reassuring smile and the crocodile's now-innocent expression, and felt a wave of relief wash over him—followed almost immediately by the distinct urge to review his clinic's patient intake policies.

"Well," he said, straightening his coat with as much dignity as he could muster, "perhaps we should reschedule for a day when Snappy is feeling less... playful."

# The Crocodile's Trick

The bell above the door jingled cheerfully, utterly failing to prepare Dr. Whitfield for what shuffled into his waiting room that Tuesday afternoon.

A crocodile.

Not a small one, either. The creature took up most of the doorway, its scaly bulk crowding past the umbrella stand, its tail sweeping a stack of magazines onto the floor. It settled into the waiting room chair—which groaned in protest—and looked at the receptionist with an expression of polite patience.

"I have an appointment," the crocodile said. "For my teeth."

Dr. Whitfield, peering out from his office door, felt his professional composure wobble. He had, in thirty years of dentistry, treated nervous children, elderly patients with dentures, and one memorable parrot with a beak infection. He had never treated a crocodile.

"Right this way," he heard himself say, because what else does one say?

The crocodile heaved himself onto the examination chair, which creaked ominously beneath his weight. Dr. Whitfield approached with his little mirror and pick, hands trembling only slightly.

"Just the front teeth to check today?" the dentist asked hopefully, eyeing the impressive rows of white daggers gleaming in the crocodile's mouth.

"Oh, no," the crocodile said, and here his eyes seemed to glint with something the dentist didn't quite trust. "It's my back teeth that ache something terrible. Right at the very back. You'll need to look deep to see them properly."

"The back teeth," Dr. Whitfield repeated faintly.

"Yes, yes." The crocodile opened his jaws wider, and wider still, until his mouth yawned like a cave, rows of teeth glistening on either side, disappearing into a dark, cavernous throat. "Go on, then. Stick your head right in. You won't see anything from out there."

Dr. Whitfield stared into that vast mouth. He thought about his mortgage. He thought about his cat, who would surely miss him. He thought about the peculiar fact that the crocodile's eyes seemed to be sparkling with barely suppressed amusement, and his scaly mouth—was that mouth *smirking*?

"Perhaps," the dentist said, voice climbing several octaves, "perhaps I could use a longer mirror instead—"

"Nonsense!" the crocodile boomed, jaws stretching impossibly wide. "Just pop your head in! It'll only take a moment!"

Sweat beaded on Dr. Whitfield's forehead. He edged closer, mirror trembling in his outstretched hand, absolutely certain that the moment his head crossed the threshold of those teeth, they would snap shut like a bear trap, and that would be the end of Dr. Reginald Whitfield, DDS, respected member of the Dental Association, beloved by no one in particular but at least *alive*.

"That's it," the crocodile encouraged, waggling what might have been an eyebrow if crocodiles had eyebrows. "Just a little closer..."

The door burst open.

"Rex! *There* you are, you naughty thing!"

A woman in a bright yellow raincoat stood in the doorway, hands on her hips, looking exasperated in the particular way of someone whose pet has slipped its leash for the third time that week.

The crocodile's mouth snapped shut with a guilty click. "...Hello, Margaret."

"Have you been bothering this poor man?" Margaret marched over and gave the crocodile a scolding tap on the snout. "I turn my back for five minutes and you go trotting off to 'get your teeth checked'! You did this to the mailman last month, didn't you? And the poor meter reader before that!"

Dr. Whitfield, who had gone quite pale and was clutching his little mirror like a shield, managed to croak, "He's... a pet?"

"Oh, he's harmless," Margaret said breezily. "Wouldn't hurt a fly. He just loves a good scare—thinks it's the funniest thing in the world, don't you, Rex?"

The crocodile had the good grace to look sheepish, insofar as a crocodile can look sheepish, which is to say not very much, but he did shift his weight and avoid the dentist's eye.

"His teeth are actually perfectly fine," Margaret continued, hooking a leash back onto the crocodile's collar. "I just can't get him to stop pulling this prank on unsuspecting professionals. Terribly sorry for the trouble."

Dr. Whitfield sat down rather suddenly in his own chair, mirror clattering to the floor. "No trouble at all," he wheezed, though his hands were still shaking. "No trouble... at all."

As Margaret led the chuckling crocodile out through the waiting room—Rex threw one last wink over his shoulder at the dentist—Dr. Whitfield made a solemn vow.

From now on, all reptilian patients would require advance paperwork. Possibly notarized. Possibly involving a full psychiatric evaluation.

And under no circumstances, *ever again*, would he stick his head anywhere near the back of anything with that many teeth.

# The Right Crocodile

In the murky waters of the Zambezi River, wildlife photographer Elena Vasquez had spent three weeks searching for the right crocodile—one whose scarred hide and ancient eyes would tell the story she wanted to capture for her documentary on Africa's apex predators.

Not just any crocodile would do. She needed one with character, with history written into every ridge of its armored skin. The young ones were too sleek, too uniform in their menace. She wanted something that looked like it had witnessed the passage of decades, maybe even centuries in reptilian time.

Her guide, Joseph, understood exactly what she meant. "There is one," he told her on the fourth week, "that the elders call Old Mabu. He has been in this stretch of river since before I was born."

They found him basking on a sandbar as the afternoon sun cast long shadows across the water. His hide bore the marks of countless battles—a missing toe here, a scar along his jaw there, evidence of a life fully lived in the brutal calculus of survival. When he opened his eyes and looked directly at her camera, Elena felt a chill that had nothing to do with the cooling evening air.

This was the right crocodile. Not because he was the largest or most dangerous, but because he embodied something true about resilience, about the quiet dignity of creatures who have endured. She spent the next two hours documenting every angle, every movement, knowing she had finally found what she'd been searching for all along.

counterfactuals.output:
**The Crocodile's Terrible Toothache**

In Wallabango, by the mucky lagoon,
Lived a crocodile named Cyril Baboon,
Who woke up one morning with terrible pain—
His tooth throbbed like thunder, again and again!

"Oh, blimey!" he bellowed. "Oh, cripes! Oh, my word!
This pain in my gob is completely absurd!
I've ninety-six teeth, each sharp as a knife,
And ALL of them hurt like they're fighting for life!"

So off waddled Cyril, all grumpy and glum,
To visit the dentist, Sir Reginald Plumb,
A man known for bravery, medals, and pluck—
Though facing a crocodile took quite a bit of luck.

"Now, open up wide," said the brave dentist chap,
As Cyril unhinged his enormous jaw-trap.
Sir Reginald peered in with light and with hook,
Then promptly turned pale and dropped both his book!

"Good gracious!" he squeaked. "What a cavern of doom!
There's a shipwreck in here, and I think there's a room!
I see several fish that are still alive—
Plus what looks suspiciously like a beehive!"

He found an old boot and a rather good hat,
A slightly squashed, soggy, deceased tabby cat,
Three spoons, a trombone, and a note that said "HELP,"
And the bones of a man who had once been called Kelp.

"Well, no wonder you're achy!" Sir Reginald cried,
"You've got a whole JUNKYARD wedged in there inside!
Let's give it a scrub and a polish and floss,
Though I fear, my dear crocodile, I'm the boss!"

He scrubbed and he polished for hours and hours,
Used forty-two toothbrushes, tanks full of showers,
Till Cyril's teeth gleamed like the moon in the night,
Ninety-six pearly-whites, sparkling and bright!

"Oh, thank you!" said Cyril. "You've saved me from doom!
No more aching molars, no more junk in my room!
I'll tell all my croc-friends how skilled you have been—"
Then he suddenly SNAPPED and swallowed the man whole again.

For you see, dear reader, though clean were his teeth,
Old habits die hard, both above and beneath.
The moral, if any, is simply just this:
Don't put your whole ARM in a crocodile's kiss.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
# The Dentist and the Crocodile

Dr. Pip was known throughout the land
As the bravest dentist, close at hand,
But even brave Pip felt a shiver of dread
When a crocodile smiled and shook its head.

"My tooth!" wept the crocodile, big fat tears,
"It's ached and it's throbbed for simply *years*!
Won't you help me, doctor, please take a peek?
I promise I'm gentle, I promise I'm meek."

Dr. Pip gulped and adjusted his hat,
"Now, crocodiles don't usually chat
So nicely to dentists—but fine, let me see,
Open up wide now, one, two, three!"

The crocodile grinned a grin so sly,
"I can't quite open it—would you mind, oh my,
Just leaning in closer, a bit more, that's right,
The tooth is right *there*, just out of sight!"

Poor Dr. Pip, so eager to please,
Leaned in close (oh, forgive him, he
Was thinking of gold stars, thinking of praise)
Right into those jaws, right into that gaze!

**SNAP!** went the crocodile, quick as a wink,
But—wait just a moment, what's this, do you think?
Dr. Pip's head was still there, still intact,
For crocodiles' teeth, as a matter of fact,

Are hollow and wobbly and rotten with decay
(That's why the poor croc was in pain all that day!)
"You tricked me!" laughed Pip, not angry, just glad,
"But your teeth are a mess—the *worst* I've had!

Now hold *very* still, no more of your tricks,
I'll fix up your smile with floss and with sticks
Of minty toothpaste, a brush, and some care—
Let's get you a smile that's healthy and fair!"

So the crocodile learned, though sneaky and bold,
That kindness beats trickery, or so I've been told,
And Dr. Pip left with his head still on straight,
A wiser (though slightly more soggy) dental mate.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a humorous narrative poem with rhyme and meter about a dentist terrified of his patient, a talking crocodile.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Dentist and the Crocodile

Dr. Milo Pierce, DDS,
Had seen most every malady,
Cavities and crooked bite,
Root canals that lost the fight—

But nothing in his dental school
Prepared him for the golden rule:
When Monday came, at half-past three,
A *crocodile* walked in for tea.

Well—not for tea. He came to see
About a toothache, aches times three,
And spoke in tones both deep and grand,
"Good day, sir. Shake my mighty hand?"

Poor Milo's own hand shook instead,
His mouth went dry, his face went red,
He eyed those teeth—a jagged wall,
Eight dozen strong, both sharp and tall.

"P-please," said Milo, "won't you sit?"
The chair groaned low beneath the fit
Of scaled and swampy crocodile
Who flashed a rather toothy smile.

"It's this back molar," Croc complained,
"The pain's been positively grained
Into my skull for one whole week—
I'd fix it myself, but pincers leak."

Now Milo held his tiny light
And peered into that yawning site,
Where teeth like stalactites hung round
Enough to make his heart astound.

He thought of nature specials seen,
Of nile banks red and rivers green,
Of *Documentaries: Nature's Bite*
And gulped, and prayed, and gripped it tight.

"Now open wide," he squeaked with fear,
The croc obliged—a jaw-drop, clear,
Revealing depths like caverns vast,
Poor Milo's courage sinking fast.

He reached in with his tiny pick,
His whole arm trembling, sight gone sick,
He found the tooth, all cracked and worn,
And croc let out a mournful moan.

"Be gentle, doc," the reptile said,
"I may look tough, but here's my dread—
I *hate* the drill, I fear the sound,
It makes my scaly skin turn 'round."

And Milo paused. His fear went still.
"You're scared? Of *me*? Despite your bill
Of fifty teeth that gleam like knives?"
The croc nodded. "Since my early lives."

So dentist small and patient grand
Sat trembling, each on equal stand,
Two frightened souls in matching fear,
Found common ground right then and there.

He fixed the tooth with gentle care,
The croc sat still (though gripped his chair),
And when 'twas done, with tears of pride,
The crocodile just up and cried:

"You're braver than you'll ever know,
To reach inside a beast's big maw!"
And Milo grinned, relief in bloom,
"You're gentler than I'd first assumed."

They shook on it—hand and claw—
Best patient-dentist bond he saw,
And Milo learned that fearsome jaws
Might house the softest, kindest cause.

So if you're ever cast with dread
Of something large, or sharp, or bred
For nightmares—pause before you flee,
It might be scared as much as thee.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
# Chompers, the Crocodile Who Went to the Dentist

In the swampy green waters of Wobbly Lagoon,
Lived a crocodile, Chompers, who howled at the moon.
He had ninety-nine teeth, sharp and gleaming and white,
But he hated the dentist with all of his might!

"I won't go!" cried Chompers, and dove for the mud,
"They'll poke and they'll prod, and it won't do me good!"
But his mama just chuckled and grabbed his front claw,
"Oh, you're going, my darling, that's dentist's law!"

So they marched through the swamp, past the lily pad throne,
To the office of Dr. Toothy P. Bone.
The waiting room buzzed with some rather odd folks—
A walrus, two beavers, all telling teeth jokes.

When they called out "Next, please!" Chompers hid 'neath a chair,
He puffed out his cheeks and refused to go there!
"I'll bite!" he announced, showing off all his teeth,
But the dentist just smiled and said, "Step on the sheet."

Dr. Bone was a heron, tall, patient, and kind,
With glasses that sparkled and a curious mind.
"Now, Chompers," she said, "let's take a quick peek,
I promise it's painless—just open your beak!"

Chompers grumbled and groaned, but he opened up wide,
And the heron leaned in with her mirror inside.
"Oh MY," she exclaimed, with a gasp and a "Whoa!"
"I've never seen anything like this before!"

Chompers froze. Was it cavities? Something more grim?
Was his mouth full of seaweed, or something too dim?
"What is it?" he mumbled, quite scared, rather meek,
"Is my breath extra stinky? Please, just let me speak!"

The heron just giggled and turned round her chair,
Held up a small mirror—"Look, see what's there!"
And nestled way back, past his ninety-nine teeth,
Sat a tiny gold minnow, blowing bubbles beneath!

"He's been hiding since Tuesday!" the fish said with cheer,
"Best hotel in the swamp—I've enjoyed my stay here!
Room service of plankton, a view of your tonsils—
Five stars, Mr. Chompers! I'll write you a chronicle!"

Everyone laughed—the nurses, his mother,
The walrus, the beavers, and each other's brother!
Chompers laughed loudest, his belly a-shaking,
"Well, THAT'S why my tummy kept rumbling and quaking!"

They gently evicted the fish from his den,
Chompers waved him off kindly, and grinned wide again.
"That wasn't so bad!" he admitted with pride,
"Next time I'll come willingly—no need to hide!"

So if you're a crocodile, scared and unsure,
Just remember old Chompers, and his dental adventure.
You never quite know what surprise you might find,
When you open up wide and let worries unwind!

**THE END** 🐊✨

# The Dentist and the Crocodile

Dr. Wilfred Winch, DDS,
Was cleaning teeth with expert ease,
When through his door, all green and grim,
A crocodile came waddling in.

Its jaws were wide, its teeth were bright,
(Which gave the dentist quite a fright)
It shuffled up and moaned, "Oh dear,
My molars ache! I'm suffering here!"

Now Dr. Winch, he dropped his drill,
His face went pale, his blood ran chill,
He tried to shout, he tried to flee,
But only managed, "Eeeeeeeek!" and "Yeeee!"

He climbed atop his dentist's chair,
He hid his head, he tore his hair,
"Don't eat me, please! I'm mostly bone!
I taste like chalk! Please leave me alone!"

The crocodile just blinked and sighed,
"I've got a cavity inside!
I only came for you to look—
Not dine on dentists like a cook!"

But Winch was far too scared to hear,
He'd wedged himself behind a chair,
And started climbing up the wall
Like some deranged, panicked squirrel.

Just then the office door flew wide,
A woman marched in, hands on side,
In floral dress and rubber boots—
"BAGSY!" she cried. "You awful brute!"

She grabbed the croc's enormous ear
And gave a tug both sharp and clear,
"You've run off THREE TIMES THIS WEEK!
You'll give this poor man a technique!"

She turned and smiled at Dr. Winch,
Who hadn't budged a single inch,
"I'm sorry, dear, he's really tame,
Old Bagsy here—that is his name.

He's had a toothache since Tuesday last,
I told him, 'Wait!' but he ran fast,
He does this every time he's sore—
He simply cannot bear the roar

Of pain inside his poor old head,
So please don't worry, don't dread—
He's soft as pudding, sweet as pie,
He wouldn't hurt a passing fly!"

Dr. Winch climbed slowly down,
Still red with fear, still wearing frown,
"You mean... he's not about to bite?"
"Good heavens, no! He's much too polite!"

So Winch, still shaking, took a peek
Inside the jaw of Mr. Meek,
And found a molar, cracked and gray,
"Aha!" he said. "I'll fix that today!"

He drilled and polished, capped it neat,
While Bagsy purred (a crocodile treat),
And when the job was finally done,
The croc grinned wide—a job well won!

"Thank you kindly!" Bagsy beamed,
(The dentist nearly fainted, screamed),
But all was well, the visit through,
And Bagsy left with molar new.

So here's the moral, plain and true:
Before you scream and turn quite blue,
Remember—crocs with aching teeth
Are sometimes gentler than beneath

Their scaly, fearsome, toothy grin,
There's just a patient checking in.
But keep this tale tucked in your head—
Best always check that they've been *fed*.
